Mildly positive on current activity and labor, but the literature points to a hawkish risk balance. Under the New Keynesian Phillips Curve framework (e.g., Galí), robust job gains and low unemployment can sustain inflation via expectations, justifying the FOMC’s emphasis on inflation risks. A Taylor-rule lens and the Bernanke–Mihov identification approach are consistent with raising the policy rate to 5.25–5.50 percent as a rule-based anti-inflation response. Research on the credit channel and the financial accelerator (Bernanke–Gertler–Gilchrist) explains why tighter bank credit will weigh on activity and inflation with uncertain magnitudes, matching the statement’s caution. The firm 2 percent objective and continued balance-sheet reduction align with forecast-based targeting principles (Svensson and Woodford) and help mitigate average inflation bias. Implementation details—lifting interest on reserve balances to 5.4 percent and operating the ON RRP at 5.3 percent—reflect modern operating frameworks discussed by Goodfriend. Banking system “soundness” trims tail risks, but overall, the mix of elevated inflation and tighter credit leaves a slightly positive yet cautious tone.
